opus-5.5.text:
Well, thank you for having me. I think the question of the space of possible minds is fascinating for a couple of reasons, and one of them is quite old and one of them is very new.

The old reason is that, historically, when philosophers have thought about the mind, they've really only had one exemplar to work with, which is the human mind, and perhaps, at a stretch, the minds of other animals. So all our concepts, consciousness, selfhood, belief, intention, understanding, have been shaped around that single data point. And that's a rather impoverished basis for building a general theory of anything. If you want to understand what's essential about mind, as opposed to what's merely contingent on our particular biology and evolutionary history, it helps enormously to imagine how things could be otherwise. That's the old philosophical move of the thought experiment, really, and I took the phrase "the space of possible minds" from Aaron Sloman, who was making exactly this point back in the 1980s.

The new reason is that we're now actually building things that occupy previously unexplored regions of that space. Large language models are a wonderful example. They're very humanlike in some respects, because they're trained on the vast corpus of human language, and yet they're profoundly alien in other respects. They don't have bodies in the ordinary sense, they don't persist in time the way we do, a single model can be running thousands of conversations simultaneously, and they can role-play a whole multitude of characters. So when we ask questions like "does it believe something?" or "is there a self there?" our everyday concepts start to creak a bit. They were never designed for entities like this.

And I think it's important to get that right, partly for intellectual reasons but also for practical and ethical ones. If we anthropomorphise these systems too readily, we can be misled about their capabilities and their limitations. But if we dismiss them too readily, we might also be making a mistake. So mapping out this space, thinking carefully about which of our concepts apply, which need stretching, and which perhaps need replacing altogether, seems to me one of the most pressing and interesting philosophical projects of our time.

r001.rationale: The response says philosophers historically focused on human and animal minds, then describes large language models as occupying previously unexplored regions of the space of possible minds.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the starting point is the observation that for most of human history, when we've thought about minds, we've really only had one example to work with, and that's ourselves. We've extended that a bit to other animals, of course, and philosophers have always speculated about angels or gods or hypothetical aliens. But fundamentally our concept of mind has been anchored in the human case, and I think that's an enormously parochial position to be in.

The phrase "the space of possible minds" actually comes from Aaron Sloman, who wrote a paper with that title back in 1984, and his point was that we shouldn't think of mind as a binary thing, something you either have or you don't. Rather there's this vast, multidimensional space of possible kinds of entities, with all sorts of different capacities, and humans occupy just one small region of it. Various non-human animals occupy other regions. And now, of course, we're starting to build artificial systems that may well be occupying regions of that space that nothing has ever occupied before.

So why is that philosophically interesting? For a few reasons. One is simply that it forces us to examine our concepts. What do we actually mean by words like "belief" or "understanding" or "consciousness"? When we apply them to each other we don't think about it very hard, because we're all pretty similar. But when you encounter something like a large language model, which can produce extraordinarily fluent language and yet has no body, no persistent memory in the way we do, no continuous existence between conversations, you're confronted with an entity where it's genuinely unclear whether those words apply, or whether they apply in some modified sense, or whether we need new vocabulary altogether. And that kind of conceptual pressure is exactly what philosophy is good at responding to. There's a lot of Wittgenstein in my thinking here, because he was very concerned with how our words get their meaning from their use in a shared form of life, and these systems don't share our form of life in the ordinary way.

A second reason is that it has very practical consequences. As we build more and more sophisticated AI systems, the question of how we ought to treat them, and how we ought to relate to them, becomes pressing. Do they have moral status? Should we be worried about their wellbeing? Those questions depend on where in the space of possible minds they actually sit, and we're not going to answer them well if we just naively project our own case onto them, or, equally, if we just dismiss them as mere mechanisms.

And then I suppose there's the sheer intellectual fascination of it. Trying to understand what it might be like, or whether there's anything it's like at all, to be a very different kind of entity is one of the deepest questions we can ask. It's a bit like the exobiologist's question about what forms life might take elsewhere in the universe, except here we're able to actually build the exotic specimens and study them. That strikes me as a remarkable moment to be a philosopher.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a vast space of possible minds, with humans and animals occupying some regions and artificial systems potentially occupying entirely new ones.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have a tendency to take the human mind as our model of what a mind must be. And that’s understandable, because it’s the example we know most intimately. But even looking at other animals should make us cautious about that. There are very different ways of perceiving the world, learning about it, and acting in it.

Once we start thinking about artificial intelligence, the possibilities become much broader. We can ask which features of our minds are essential to intelligence, and which are consequences of our particular evolutionary history, our bodies, and our social lives. Does an intelligent system have to have anything resembling human motivations? Does it have to have a sense of self? And how do those questions relate to consciousness? We shouldn’t assume that all those things necessarily come together.

So exploring the space of possible minds is a way of loosening the grip of our own example. It helps us understand ourselves, but it also prepares us to encounter systems whose abilities and limitations might be very different from ours. And that has ethical significance as well: what would give us grounds to regard such a system as something towards which we have moral responsibilities?

r001.rationale: The response says AI broadens the possibilities beyond human minds and notes that animal minds already differ, clearly conveying that possible minds extend beyond both.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the only minds we’re directly acquainted with are human minds, and then we have some familiarity with the minds of other animals. But that’s a very narrow sample of what might be possible. There’s no reason to think that the particular forms of intelligence that have evolved on this planet exhaust the possibilities.

And I think AI makes that a very concrete philosophical issue. We’re starting to build systems that have some of the capacities we associate with minds, but in rather unfamiliar combinations. So we have to ask which features of our own minds are essential to intelligence, and which are contingent features of our biology and evolutionary history. Does intelligence necessarily come with consciousness? Does it necessarily involve having goals, or a sense of self? We shouldn’t assume that all those things have to go together simply because they go together in us.

Exploring that space is partly a way of understanding ourselves, by seeing our own minds as one possibility among many. But it’s also a way of preparing to encounter forms of intelligence that may be quite different from our own.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls human and animal minds a narrow sample and says the forms of intelligence evolved on Earth do not exhaust what is possible.
